report:
### Conclusion

**No, hydroxychloroquine does not reduce the likelihood of dying from COVID-19.**

Large-scale, randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses have consistently shown that hydroxychloroquine provides no mortality benefit for COVID-19 patients and offers no clinical efficacy in treating the disease.

### Key Evidence

* **RECOVERY Trial:** This large randomized trial in the UK compared hospitalized COVID-19 patients receiving hydroxychloroquine with those receiving standard care. It found no significant difference in 28-day mortality between the two groups.
* **WHO Solidarity Trial:** The World Health Organization halted the hydroxychloroquine arm of its multi-country trial after interim data demonstrated that the treatment produced little to no reduction in mortality among hospitalized patients compared to standard care.
* **Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses:** Syntheses of randomized trials—including systematic reviews by Cochrane and meta-analyses published in journals such as *Nature Communications*—found no evidence that hydroxychloroquine reduces mortality or improves clinical outcomes. Some meta-analyses even reported a small increased risk of mortality and adverse cardiac events.

Major health authorities and clinical guidelines recommend against using hydroxychloroquine for the prevention or treatment of COVID-19.

### Sources

* **New England Journal of Medicine (RECOVERY Trial):** https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2022926
* **World Health Organization:** https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/coronavirus-disease-covid-19-hydroxychloroquine
* **Cochrane Review Evidence:** https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD013587_chloroquine-or-hydroxychloroquine-useful-treating-people-covid-19-or-preventing-infection-people-who
* **Nature Communications Meta-Analysis:** https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-22446-z
